title: Hierarchical key-affinity TTL controller and safe apply plan
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: Design and implement a hierarchical key-affinity TTL controller that produces per-prefix TTL recommendations informed by a batching-aware hit-rate model, plus an automated safe-apply/rollback orchestration. Goal is to reduce per-token serving cost by reclaiming effective cache hit value while bounding tail latency and cold-start risk.

Problem statement: Current global TTL heuristics are brittle for workloads with nested prefix structure (model+route+user cohort). We observe both under-caching (lost cost savings) and over-caching (memory churn on GPU nodes) because heuristics ignore batching dynamics and prefix affinity. This ticket builds a controller that: (1) models prefix hit probability conditioned on batching window and request inter-arrival, (2) recommends a TTL ladder across a prefix hierarchy, (3) stages safe applies with shadow runs/canaries and automated rollback triggers.

Modeling approach: Use a sampling-based estimator that constructs a per-prefix semi-Markov access model: state = {last-access-age, batch-window-bucket, prefix-depth}. The estimator consumes request traces with batching alignment to estimate P(hit | TTL, batch-window). We then compute expected token-savings and expected memory-pressure per candidate TTL. Candidate TTLs are prioritized by a utility score: utility = expected_token_savings - lambda * eviction_cost. Lambda is configurable per deployment tier.

Key-affinity and hierarchy: Keys are organized into a three-level hierarchy (model:route:cohort). Rather than recommend independent TTLs for every leaf, the controller computes TTL gradients across hierarchy levels and enforces smoothness priors so sibling prefixes inherit base TTLs unless statistically justified. This reduces churn and mitigates noisy low-traffic prefixes from influencing global cache behavior.

Batching-aware adjustments: The hit estimator explicitly models batching window distribution (observed effective batching latency and batch sizes). The recommended TTL for a prefix increases when effective-batch-size distribution yields high intra-batch locality (higher chance of hits within a single request's KV lifetime). Conversely, for prefixes with low batching affinity we bias recommendations toward lower TTL to avoid memory churn.

Safe apply and rollback plan: 1) Dry-run and shadow: compute recommendations and apply in shadow mode for 24h (no eviction), collect metrics. 2) Canary: apply TTL deltas to a tiny percentage (0.5%) of traffic on a small set of nodes with tight monitoring. 3) Cohort ramp: expand to 5% then 25% using geometric steps. 4) Full apply: remaining traffic. Rollback triggers: immediate rollback if 5m hit-rate delta < -3% AND token-cost increase > 2% OR p99 latency regresses > 10% relative to baseline. Additionally, safety gates include per-prefix max-TTL caps and per-node eviction rate throttles. Automatic rollback is executed by orchestration if any gate breaches for more than two consecutive evaluation windows.

Telemetry and observability required: add per-prefix metrics (rolling 5m hit_rate, effective_batch_size_histogram, per-prefix token_savings_estimate), per-node metrics (eviction_rate, memory_pressure_pct), and global signals (aggregate token-spend, tail latency P50/P95/P99). Dashboards and alerts must be created before canary.

Trade-offs and constraints: - Aggressive TTLs save tokens but increase eviction churn and risk higher cold miss latency for rare but important prefixes. - Smoothness priors reduce noise but can under-optimize high-value leaf prefixes. We choose conservative lambda defaults to bias toward stability for enterprise customers.

Deliverables: controller service, simulation harness, rollout orchestrator hooks, dashboards, runbook with rollback playbook, and a postmortem checklist for out-of-band incidents.

decisions: Use hierarchical TTL recommendations with smoothness priors to reduce noisy leaf churn
Model must explicitly account for batching window distribution (not just per-request rates)
Automated rollback will be driven by composite gates (hit-rate, cost, latency) evaluated on 5m windows
Conservative default lambda for enterprise clusters; aggressive tuning opt-in via per-customer knob
risks: Mis-estimated prefix affinity could cause token-spend regressions if hot prefixes are under-cached
High eviction churn may increase memory pressure on smaller dedicated pools
False positives in anomaly detectors could cause unnecessary rollbacks if windows are too narrow
Complexity of per-prefix metrics may increase cardinality and observability costs
acceptance_criteria: Controller computes TTL recommendations and stores candidate diffs in config store
Simulation harness reproduces production-like token-savings and worst-case latency scenarios with trace replay
Telemetry panels show per-prefix hit_rate, effective_batch_size distribution, token_savings_estimate
Canary stage performs automated rollback on gate violations and operator can trigger manual revert
PR merged and basic e2e test against shadow traffic passes
